entries.source_title: Il/elle/ils/elles = it/he/she/they (French Subject Pronouns)
entries.evidence: The pronoun inventory and contrasting book/table and all-female/mixed-group examples teach grammatical reference; items require elle, elles, il and ils for new referents.

entries.source_title: On can mean either we/one/people (French Subject Pronouns)
entries.evidence: On is explicitly taught as conversational we, generic people and an unspecified person, always with a singular verb; items test the singular form and reject an exclusively we interpretation.

entries.source_title: Using nous/vous/ils/elles to replace compound subjects (French Subject Pronouns)
entries.evidence: Compound-subject rules prioritise the speaker, then the listener, then third-person gender; exercises replace Hugo et moi, ta sœur et toi and a mixed third-person group.

entries.source_title: Nous vs on to say "we" in French (French Subject Pronouns)
entries.evidence: The section contrasts conversational on parle with nous parlons and explains register and verb agreement; check and review items transform the same we-reference in both directions.

entries.source_title: "C'est" vs "Il/Elle est" to say it is/she is/he is in French
entries.evidence: Identification with a determined noun phrase is contrasted with a bare profession or description of a known referent; exercises select c'est, il est and the correct descriptive subject.

entries.source_title: C'est, ce sont = this is, these are (French Demonstrative Pronouns)
entries.evidence: C'est and careful plural ce sont are taught with names and singular/plural noun phrases, alongside the spoken c'est-plus-plural caveat; items practise both numbers.

entries.source_title: Ça = that/this/it (French Demonstrative Pronouns)
entries.evidence: Ça is explicitly taught as a broad demonstrative subject or object with singular agreement and informal register; items replace cela and supply the subject of marche.

entries.source_title: Moi/toi/lui/elle = Me/you/him/her - simple cases (French Stress Pronouns)
entries.evidence: The complete stressed inventory introduces moi/toi/lui/elle, independent answers and prepositional uses; exercises require moi, lui and toi rather than subject forms.

entries.source_title: Nous/vous/eux/elles = Us/you/them - simple cases (French Stress Pronouns)
entries.evidence: The section explicitly distinguishes stressed nous/vous/eux/elles, including all-feminine versus mixed groups; tasks require eux, nous and elles after prepositions.

entries.source_title: Penser que/Croire que = To think that/To believe that in French
entries.evidence: Penser que and croire que introduce a complete indicative idea, with mandatory que/qu' and a contrast with penser à; items join clauses, conjugate penser and restore qu'.

entries.source_title: Me/te/nous/vous = Me/you/us/you (French Direct and Indirect Object Pronouns)
entries.evidence: Direct and indirect objects are defined in French, with me/te/nous/vous placement, elision and infinitive attachment; exercises test both object types and their position.

entries.source_title: Tout le monde = Everybody/Everyone (French Indefinite Pronouns)
entries.evidence: Tout le monde is explicitly a collective meaning with singular grammatical agreement; an insertion and an error correction require singular verbs.

entries.source_title: Conjugate avoir in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: The full six-person avoir paradigm is taught and applied to possession and fixed expressions; items retrieve singular, plural and elided forms.

entries.source_title: Conjugate être in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: The complete être paradigm and identity/state uses are visible; separate items retrieve every person, including polite vous and singular on.

entries.source_title: Conjugate aller in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: All six present forms of irregular aller are taught with destination examples; items retrieve vas, vais, allons, vont and va.

entries.source_title: Conjugate venir/tenir and derivatives in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Complete venir/tenir paradigms and explicit derivative transfer teach -ien/-en/-ienn stems; exercises include revenir, retenir, obtenir and devenir as well as the base verbs.

entries.source_title: Conjugate regular -er verbs in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: The regular -er stem and six endings are shown, including silent endings and the aller exception; retrieval and correction use several regular verbs and subjects.

entries.source_title: Expressing current actions, habits and situations (English Present Tense) with the present tense (Le Présent) in French
entries.evidence: Paired current-state, routine and now examples explain the French present's multiple English readings; items test a repeated Monday habit and simple/continuous equivalence.

entries.source_title: Conjugate faire in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: The complete faire paradigm is taught for do/make and fixed activity uses; exercises retrieve every person including faites and font.

entries.source_title: Conjugate vouloir in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Vouloir's full present paradigm and direct infinitive construction are visible; exercises test singular and plural stem changes.

entries.source_title: Conjugate pouvoir in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Pouvoir's full present paradigm, ability/permission meanings and formal puis caveat are taught; exercises retrieve plural stems and retain a following infinitive.

entries.source_title: Conjugate devoir in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: The complete devoir paradigm is taught with obligation examples; items require doit, devons and doivent.

entries.source_title: Conjugate regular -ir verbs in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Finir's complete paradigm explains the plural -iss- family and excludes unrelated -ir verbs; tasks cover finir, choisir and réussir and the limit of the pattern.

entries.source_title: Conjugate regular -dre verbs in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Vendre's complete paradigm teaches retention of d and no added third-person t, with explicit irregular-family limits; exercises transfer to répondre, attendre and rendre.

entries.source_title: Conjugate croire in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: All present croire forms show y only with nous/vous and i elsewhere; exercises retrieve croyons, croient, croyez and croit.

entries.source_title: Conjugate semi-regular -cer verbs in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: The full commencer paradigm explains ç before -ons but not before e; items contrast nous commençons/avançons with vous commencez.

entries.source_title: Conjugate semi-regular -ger verbs in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: The full manger paradigm and a partager example explain the sound-preserving e before -ons; both base and derivative-family tasks require it.

entries.source_title: Conjugate reflexive verbs in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: The reflexive subject/pronoun/verb pattern, all pronouns and elision are explicitly taught; items select the matching pronoun and distinguish reflexive from non-reflexive meaning.

entries.source_title: Conjugate reflexive verb se réveiller in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: A complete se réveiller paradigm and wake-versus-get-up contrast teach the verb, not just an incidental routine example; items require singular and plural reflexive phrases.

entries.source_title: Conjugate reflexive verb se lever in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: The complete se lever paradigm explicitly contrasts è forms with unchanged nous/vous stems; exercises require se lève and nous levons.

entries.source_title: Conjugate reflexive verb se coucher in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Se coucher is defined as going to bed and shown across all persons; exercises retrieve nous couchons and se couche with the proper pronouns.

entries.source_title: Conjugate reflexive verb s'habiller in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: The full s'habiller paradigm explains silent-h elision and getting-dressed meaning; tasks require t'habilles and s'habille.

entries.source_title: Conjugate reflexive verb se laver in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Se laver has a complete paradigm and an explicit body-part article rule; exercises require the correct reflexive pronoun and vous lavez les mains.

entries.source_title: Conjugate reflexive verb s'amuser in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: S'amuser is explained as a conventional pronominal meaning with a full paradigm; items contrast elided s'amusent with non-elided nous amusons.

entries.source_title: Conjugate -é(-)er, -e(-)er verbs - except -eter and -eler - in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Complete lever and préférer paradigms show e/é becoming è before silent endings; exercises cover both changing stems and preserved vous é.

entries.source_title: Conjugate partir/sortir and other irregular -TIR verbs in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Full partir/sortir paradigms and mentir forms teach the short singular/full plural pattern; exercises include repartir and mentir rather than assuming all -tir verbs are regular.

entries.source_title: Conjugate -eter and -eler verbs in the present tense in French (Le Présent) - main rule (ll / tt)
entries.evidence: Full appeler/jeter paradigms explicitly teach consonant doubling before silent endings, unchanged nous/vous and derivative transfer; items include rappeler/rejeter.

entries.source_title: Conjugate prendre and derivatives in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Prendre, apprendre and comprendre have complete patterns and derivative guidance, including no plural d and third-plural nn; tasks also cover reprendre and surprendre.

entries.source_title: Expressing ongoing actions (English Present Continuous) with the present tense (Le Présent) in French
entries.evidence: The present is explicitly contrasted with an incorrect être-plus-present imitation of English continuous; two items identify the valid ongoing-action construction.

entries.source_title: Conjugate dire and derivatives in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Dire and redire paradigms contrast dites/redites with interdisez/prédisez/contredisez/médisez and maudire's -iss- plural; exercises address every named exception family.

entries.source_title: Conjugate dormir and other -MIR verbs in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Dormir's full present paradigm explicitly restores m in plural forms and excludes finir-style -iss-; tasks retrieve dormez and dort.

entries.source_title: Conjugate écrire/inscrire in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Écrire and inscrire have full present patterns with plural v, and décrire is mapped to the same family; exercises retrieve singular and plural forms.

entries.source_title: Expressing immediate and near-future actions with the present tense (Le Présent) in French
entries.evidence: Future-oriented present uses are explicitly explained through scheduled, planned and immediate actions; exercises identify future meaning and construct partons with demain.

entries.source_title: Conjugate verbs in the near future in French using aller + infinitive (Le Futur Proche)
entries.evidence: The full aller-plus-infinitive paradigm explains intention/expectation, no fixed distance limit and negation; tasks construct several subjects and an unchanged infinitive.

entries.source_title: Conjugate lire in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Lire has a complete present paradigm with singular lit versus plural lis- forms; exercises retrieve lit, lisent and lisons.

entries.source_title: Conjugate reflexive verbs in the near future in French using aller + infinitive (Le Futur Proche)
entries.evidence: A full reflexive future paradigm explains pronoun placement after aller, matching person and elision; items construct and negate reflexive future phrases and repair pronoun order.

entries.source_title: Expressing the close past in French using "venir de" + [infinitive] (Le Passé Proche)
entries.evidence: Venir de has a complete six-person paradigm and explicit recent-completion meaning, elision and reflexive placement; exercises construct forms rather than merely naming the tense.

entries.source_title: Conjugate mettre and derivatives in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Mettre's complete pattern and full permettre/promettre derivative patterns show one singular t versus plural tt; items cover putting, allowing, promising and putting back.

entries.source_title: Conjugate -eter and -eler verbs in the present tense in French (Le Présent) - with "è"
entries.evidence: Acheter and geler have complete è paradigms, contrasted with appeler/jeter and accepted rectified variants such as épèle; exercises test both è families and variant recognition.

entries.source_title: Conjugate reflexive verb s'asseoir in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Both accepted six-person s'asseoir present series are shown, with sitting-down meaning and the assoir spelling note; answer keys accept both legitimate series.

entries.source_title: Conjugate boire in the present tense in French (Le Présent)
entries.evidence: Boire's full paradigm teaches boi-/buv-/boiv- stems; tasks retrieve singular and both plural stem types.

entries.source_title: Du/de la/de l'/des = Some/any (French Partitive Articles)
entries.evidence: Unspecified quantities are explicitly taught with du/de la/de l'/des, including their distinction from category le and counted un; all four quantity forms are exercised.

entries.source_title: Definite articles contract with à and de in French (French Contracted Articles)
entries.evidence: The four à/de plus le/les contractions and the non-contraction of la/l' are explained with original examples; exercises require aux, du, à l' and des.

entries.source_title: Continents/countries/counties/regions/states are masculine, feminine or plural in French (Gender)
entries.evidence: Country, continent, region and state names are explicitly listed with gender/number, final-e exceptions and articleless cases; exercises test masculine Canada/Mexique and elided Afrique.

entries.source_title: Using le, la, l', les with continents, countries & regions names (definite articles)
entries.evidence: The section explains retaining conventional articles when geographical names serve as subjects or direct objects, versus their prepositional constructions; the items test both sentence roles.

entries.source_title: En/l'/au with seasons (French Articles and Prepositions)
entries.evidence: All four season nouns and au printemps/en été/en automne/en hiver are taught, together with definite-article seasonal time phrases; exercises include the l'été alternative.

entries.source_title: Using le, la, l', les before nouns when generalising (definite articles)
entries.evidence: A general preference explicitly takes a definite category article, contrasted with an unspecified portion and one serving; recognition and constructed-review items require le pain and la musique after aimer.

entries.source_title: Identifying the gender of nouns by some specific word endings in French
entries.evidence: Gender clues in -tion/-sion/-ment/-age are taught with named exceptions and the warning that final e is not decisive; tasks apply a clue and recognise exceptions.

entries.source_title: Using "le" with days of the week + the weekend (French Definite Articles)
entries.evidence: Particular lundi is contrasted with habitual le lundi, and le week-end with ce week-end; items require the article for a weekly habit and recurring weekend activity.

entries.source_title: Using le, la, les with weights and measures (definite articles)
entries.evidence: Prices per kilo, per item and per hundred grams explicitly use le/la/les; examples and exercises test singular and plural rate units.

entries.source_title: Forming the plural of French nouns ending in -au or -eau
entries.evidence: The usual -eau/-au + x patterns are contrasted with landau/sarrau exceptions; exercises include cadeaux, tuyaux and landaus.

entries.source_title: Using le, la, les with body parts and clothing (definite articles)
entries.evidence: Body-part and clothing definite articles are explicitly tied to a clear owner, without extending the rule to every clothing sentence; items test les dents in a reflexive action and les poches in the familiar hands-in-pockets description.

entries.source_title: Using le, la, les with titles, languages and academic subjects (definite articles)
entries.evidence: Languages and subjects as nouns, bare language after parler, and professional titles when mentioning versus addressing are explained; exercises test les mathématiques and le professeur Laurent.

entries.source_title: Forming the plural of French nouns ending in -al
entries.evidence: The -al → -aux family is taught alongside common -als exceptions; journaux, festivals and bals are explicitly exercised.

entries.source_title: Forming the plural of French nouns ending in -eu
entries.evidence: The usual -eu + x pattern and pneu/bleu exceptions are visible; exercises contrast jeux with pneus.

entries.source_title: Surnames don't pluralise in French
entries.evidence: Ordinary family surnames are taught as unchanged, with a historical/dynastic caveat; three tasks prevent English -s and common-noun -eaux overgeneralisation.

entries.source_title: Adjectives ending with mute -e don't change in the feminine in French
entries.evidence: An existing silent final e is explicitly retained without an additional feminine e, with calm/quiet-street examples; tasks supply feminine calme and feminine plural utiles without an extra e.

entries.source_title: Colour descriptions change according to gender and number (French Colour Adjectives)
entries.evidence: Simple colour agreement is contrasted with compound colours and noun-colour invariability, including exceptions rose/mauve; tasks test vertes, bleu clair, orange and blanches.

entries.source_title: Standalone adjectives after c'est are always masculine
entries.evidence: Masculine singular is explicitly limited to a standalone impersonal c'est evaluation, not an adjective inside a following feminine noun phrase; items test both sides of that distinction.

entries.source_title: Expressing possession in French with "de"
entries.evidence: Thing + de + owner is taught as the French alternative to English apostrophe-s, with elision/contractions; items construct le vélo de Paul and des voisins.

entries.source_title: Mon, ma, mes; ton, ta, tes; son, sa, ses = my; your; his / her in French (French possessive adjectives)
entries.evidence: Mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes and son/sa/ses are explicitly selected by the possessed noun, with feminine vowel/silent-h forms; tasks test gender, number, elision and owner ambiguity.

entries.source_title: Notre / nos / votre / vos / leur / leurs = our / your / their (French Possessive Adjectives)
entries.evidence: Notre/nos, votre/vos and leur/leurs are taught for plural owners and polite vous, with possessed-item number controlling the form; all six forms are exercised.

entries.source_title: Forming the feminine of nouns and adjectives ending in "-ien/-ion/-on" in French
entries.evidence: The section explicitly teaches -ien/-on adjective pairs and animate -ion noun pairs, with examples of musician, champion and lioness; exercises require canadienne, championne and bonne without inventing feminines for object nouns.

entries.source_title: Adjectives ending in -eux become -euse in the feminine in French
entries.evidence: The -eux → -euse family is taught with happy/serious examples and distinguished from other -x pairs; exercises require heureuse and heureuses.

entries.source_title: Adjectives ending in -s or -x change in the plural forms only when feminine in French
entries.evidence: Masculine final s/x adjectives remain unchanged in plural while their feminine forms add plural s; items contrast bas with feminine plural heureuses.

entries.source_title: Beau, nouveau, vieux, fou, mou have two masculine forms and one feminine form (French Adjectives)
entries.evidence: Beau/bel/belle, nouveau/nouvel/nouvelle, vieux/vieil/vieille, fou/fol/folle and mou/mol/molle are explicitly taught, with fol/mol labelled literary recognition; tasks test ordinary and recognition forms.

entries.source_title: Neuf vs nouveau to say new in French
entries.evidence: Nouveau as new-to-the-situation is contrasted with unused neuf, with a second-hand bicycle example and the neuve/neufs/neuves forms; items test meaning and agreement.

entries.source_title: Forming regular adverbs with "-ment" in French (French Adverbs)
entries.evidence: Regular feminine-plus-ment formation, direct attachment after common vowel endings and invariable placement are taught with meaningful adjective/adverb contrasts; multiple original constructions retrieve the forms.

entries.source_title: Forming the feminine of adjectives ending in "-el/-eil/-il/-ul/-et/some in -s" in French
entries.evidence: Named -el/-eil/-il/-ul/-et and selected -s pairs are taught without a blanket doubling rule; tasks cover naturelle, pareille, gentille, nulle, grosse, complète, civile and nette.

entries.source_title: Beau, nouveau, vieux have different plural forms for masculine and feminine (French Adjectives)
entries.evidence: Masculine beaux/nouveaux/vieux and feminine belles/nouvelles/vieilles are explicitly listed and exemplified; items retrieve masculine beaux/vieux and feminine nouvelles.

entries.source_title: Adjectives ending in -er become -ère in the feminine in French
entries.evidence: The -er → -ère change is explicitly taught with léger, cher and dernier, plus an original légère example; check and review retrieve chère and légères.

entries.source_title: Position of French Adjectives - More adjectives that go BEFORE nouns
entries.evidence: A named list of familiar pre-noun adjectives is contrasted with normal post-noun colour/nationality descriptions and a meaning-sensitive grand example; tasks place petite/rouge and apply the careful de-before-adjective pattern.

entries.source_title: Ne ... pas = Not - with simple tenses (French Negations)
entries.evidence: Ne/n' and pas surround a simple conjugated verb, with an explicit spoken-ne caveat; tasks transform consonant and silent-h statements.

entries.source_title: Un/une become de/d' in negative sentences in French (French Indefinite Articles)
entries.evidence: Ordinary negative indefinite quantities use de/d', with être and explicit-contrast exceptions explained; exercises test a denied singular/plural quantity and retained un after être.

entries.source_title: Du/de la/de l'/des all become de/d' in negative sentences (French Partitive Articles)
entries.evidence: The partitive forms become de/d' for ordinary denied quantities while definite categories remain; items test soup, oil and the preserved article for a cheese preference.

entries.source_title: Using "si" instead of "oui" to disagree with a negative question or statement in French
entries.evidence: Si explicitly contradicts a negative assumption, while non can confirm the negative; tasks require si when the person does come or does own a car.

entries.source_title: Ne ... jamais = Never (French Negations)
entries.evidence: Ne…jamais replaces ne…pas for never, with simple and reflexive examples; tasks construct both patterns without adding pas.

entries.source_title: Non plus = Neither/nor (French Negations)
entries.evidence: Non plus is explicitly contrasted with positive aussi and illustrated as an independent stressed-pronoun response and clause addition; tasks construct moi non plus and append non plus to a complete negative sentence.

entries.source_title: Ne ... pas = Not - with reflexive verbs in simple tenses (French Negations)
entries.evidence: The reflexive pronoun stays between ne and the conjugated verb; exercises construct negative se lever and se coucher statements.

entries.source_title: Position of French Negations - with conjugated verb + infinitive
entries.evidence: Negating a conjugated verb plus infinitive is contrasted with negating only the infinitive, explaining both ne…pas placement and ne pas together; tasks exercise each scope.

entries.source_title: C'est quoi, Qu'est-ce que c'est ? = What's that? (French Questions)
entries.evidence: Neutral qu'est-ce que c'est and conversational c'est quoi are explicitly taught as identification questions with paired answers; tasks construct both.

entries.source_title: Asking yes/no questions in French with intonation, est-ce que, n'est-ce pas (French Questions)
entries.evidence: Statement-order intonation, est-ce que/qu' and fixed confirmation n'est-ce pas are explained and contrasted; tasks produce all three patterns.

entries.source_title: Asking questions in French with "qui/que/quoi/quand/où/comment/pourquoi/combien" (French Question Words)
entries.evidence: Every named question word has an explicit meaning and original example; exercises cover qui, que, quoi, quand, où, comment, pourquoi and combien de/d'.

entries.source_title: Dans/sur/sous/devant/derrière/entre = in/on top of/under/in front of/behind/between (French Prepositions of Location)
entries.evidence: Dans/sur/sous/devant/derrière/entre are explicitly defined and spatially contrasted; one constrained exercise retrieves each preposition.

entries.source_title: En vs Dans with locations (French Prepositions of Location)
entries.evidence: Established en expressions for setting/activity are contrasted with dans plus a specific physical noun phrase; items distinguish en classe from dans cette ville.

entries.source_title: À côté de, en face de, à l'extérieur de, à l'intérieur de, près de, loin de, au coin de (French Prepositions)
entries.evidence: All seven named compound prepositions are explained with retained de and contraction rules; tasks exercise near, next to, opposite, far, inside, outside and corner forms.

entries.source_title: Pour + [infinitive] = In order to + [do] in French
entries.evidence: Pour + infinitive expresses the same subject's purpose and is contrasted with a desire and a separate-subject clause; items retain an infinitive and combine an action with its purpose.

entries.source_title: En/au/aux = In/to with countries and continents (French Prepositions)
entries.evidence: Country/continent destination and location use en, au or aux by the established gender/number/vowel construction; tasks include feminine France, plural États-Unis and masculine vowel-initial Iran.

entries.source_title: En/Dans = in/to + regions/states/counties (French Prepositions)
entries.evidence: Regional/state/county constructions are explicitly learned by usage, with en Californie, dans le Yorkshire and accepted au/dans state variants; exercises test those distinctions without rejecting dans le Texas.

entries.source_title: À = To/in and De = From/of with cities in French (French Prepositions of Location)
entries.evidence: Ordinary cities take à/de, while an article belonging to a name is retained and can contract; tasks cover Lyon, Paris and Le Havre.

entries.source_title: Venir de/d'/du/des = To come/be from with countries/states/regions and continents (French Prepositions)
entries.evidence: Origin constructions de/d'/du/des are explicitly taught for countries, continents and regions with named examples and Québec city/province distinction; exercises retrieve each relevant origin type.

entries.source_title: À/en + [means of transportation] (French Prepositions)
entries.evidence: Transport-mode en and conventional à expressions are contrasted with physical vehicle location and regional variants; tasks test plane, walking, car, horse and train forms.

entries.source_title: Differences between French and English usages - Using "dans" with streets and means of transportation (French Prepositions of Location)
entries.evidence: Dans le bus versus English on the bus and dans la rue for street activity are explicitly explained, not inferred from examples; tasks target each English/French difference.

entries.source_title: À + [heure] = At + [time] in French
entries.evidence: À introduces event times and contrasts with il est for the current time; exercises require à midi and à minuit, alongside numbered-time teaching.

entries.source_title: Chez = at someone's place (French Prepositions)
entries.evidence: Chez introduces a person, home or professional practice and takes stressed pronouns; tasks contrast named people, chez moi and a building's à construction.

entries.source_title: Compound nouns formed with prepositions à/de/en in French
entries.evidence: Noun compounds explicitly contrast purpose/type with à, contents with de and material with en; tasks test cups, wood, toothbrushes and a glass of water.

entries.source_title: Compound nouns formed with [noun] + à + [infinitive] in French
entries.evidence: Noun + à + infinitive names an object's function, with washing-machine, dining-room and sewing-machine examples; tasks keep the function verb infinitive.

entries.source_title: Telling time in French - general 12-hour clock rules
entries.evidence: The 12-hour system explains heure(s), midi/minuit, quarter/half past and minutes to the next hour, including demi/demie; tasks construct the main forms.

entries.source_title: Expressing numbers 70 to 999 in French
entries.evidence: Numbers 70–999 are built from explicit tens/teens rules, cent/vingt agreement and named regional variants; exercises test 70, 81, 200, 999, 80 and regional validity.

entries.source_title: Expressing large numbers -thousands/millions/billions - in French
entries.evidence: Mille invariability and million/milliard noun behaviour are taught, including English billion and de before a counted noun; exercises test each distinction.

entries.source_title: Writing decimal numbers in French
entries.evidence: French decimal commas and preserved zero digits are explicitly taught with reading alternatives and thousands grouping; exercises write 4,07 and read 2,05 with its zero.

entries.source_title: Telling time in French - 24-hour clock rules = AM vs PM
entries.evidence: The 24-hour system uses direct minute counts, h notation and conversion from a.m./p.m.; exercises read two schedule times and convert 8 p.m. to 20 h.

entries.source_title: An vs année, matin vs matinée, jour vs journée, soir vs soirée to express a time unit or a duration in French
entries.evidence: All four unit/duration pairs are explicitly explained with gender, age, time-point and whole-period examples plus exceptions to an absolute counting rule; tasks cover every pair.

entries.source_title: Ordinal numbers - 1st/2nd/10th/etc - in French
entries.evidence: Ordinals teach premier/première, regular -ième, spelling changes cinq/neuf, compound unième and second/seconde; exercises target the key formation decisions.

entries.source_title: Ordinal vs Cardinal numbers - Differences between French and English usages
entries.evidence: The section distinguishes ordinal rank from cardinal labels for pages, lessons, monarchs and most dates; tasks contrast a cardinal page label with ordinal rank and transform a numbered door label into la neuvième porte.

entries.source_title: Expressing timeliness in French - late/early/on time - general
entries.evidence: En retard/en avance/à l'heure are explained relative to a schedule, with à temps for a useful deadline and de for an amount; exercises use concrete timing situations.

entries.source_title: Expressing how you are with aller (Greetings in French)
entries.evidence: Aller is explicitly taught for well-being rather than physical movement, with polite/familiar questions and ça va; tasks select replies and form the greeting.

entries.source_title: Talking about the weather in French - il fait + [adjectif]
entries.evidence: Impersonal singular il fait introduces weather adjectives and temperatures, contrasted with personal avoir sensations; tasks test fait, beau, frais and the impersonal form.

entries.source_title: Talking about the weather in French - il y a + [nom]
entries.evidence: Il y a introduces explicitly gendered weather nouns with articles and stays singular before plurals; tasks test quantities, plural clouds and negative de.

entries.source_title: Faire de/jouer à : talking about sports, hobbies and leisure activities in French
entries.evidence: Faire de and jouer à are taught with sports/games, article contractions and legitimate overlap such as tennis; items test both constructions and all article shapes.

entries.source_title: Jouer de = to play an instrument in French
entries.evidence: Jouer de for instruments is explicitly contrasted with jouer à for games, including du/de la/de l' and the faire-du-piano alternative; tasks retrieve instrument constructions.

entries.source_title: Ça m'est égal = I don't mind/care (French Idiomatic Expressions)
entries.evidence: Ça m'est égal is taught as no preference in an appropriate minor-choice context, with tone cautions and all person-pronoun forms; tasks test meaning, elision and singular est.

entries.source_title: Avoir besoin de = To need (French Expressions with avoir)
entries.evidence: Avoir besoin de has a complete avoir pattern, noun/infinitive complements and mass/count/identified-object distinctions; tasks test the construction and its article choices.

entries.source_title: Avoir envie de = To feel like, want to (French Expressions with avoir)
entries.evidence: Avoir envie de is explicitly a desire or feeling-like construction, contrasted with a need and obligation; exercises require de, select envie for the intended meaning and conjugate avoir.

entries.source_title: Faire les courses vs Faire les magasins to talk about shopping (French Expressions with faire)
entries.evidence: Faire les courses is taught for groceries/everyday necessities and faire les magasins for visiting/browsing shops, with context and variant cautions; items test meaning and faire forms.

entries.source_title: Devoir vs Avoir besoin de to express "to need to" in French
entries.evidence: The section explicitly contrasts devoir + direct infinitive for an obligation with avoir besoin de for a need, acknowledging overlap; exercises distinguish complement formation and an explicitly stated personal need.

entries.source_title: Expressing possession in French with "être à"
entries.evidence: Être à + name or stressed pronoun is explicitly contrasted with a de-owner noun phrase; tasks express ownership and agree être with plural possessed things.

entries.source_title: Être d'accord avec = to agree with (French Expressions with être)
entries.evidence: The full être d'accord paradigm, avec + person, sur + topic and invariable accord are taught; tasks cover formation, preposition, stressed pronoun and negation.

entries.source_title: Avoir mal (à) = To be in pain, to hurt somewhere (French Expressions with avoir)
entries.evidence: Avoir mal à locates a symptom with definite body-part articles, distinguished from être malade; exercises require au, à la, aux and à l' and identify a located pain.

entries.source_title: Describing senses with "sentir" - The different meanings of the verb "sentir" in French
entries.evidence: Sentir has a full paradigm and explicit perception, emitted-smell and reflexive-state meanings, plus invariable bon; exercises test constructions and meaning rather than just verb spelling.

entries.source_title: Expressing ongoing actions in the present in French with "être en train de"
entries.evidence: Être en train de has a full paradigm, ongoing-process meaning, ordinary-present/state limits and reflexive placement; tasks construct it and distinguish ongoing from just-completed action.

entries.source_title: Avoir peur de = To be afraid/scared of (French Expressions with avoir)
entries.evidence: Avoir peur de explicitly takes a noun or infinitive and keeps peur unchanged; exercises retrieve avoir, combine de + les and correct an être substitution.

entries.source_title: Ça y est = That's it/It's done (French Idiomatic Expressions)
entries.evidence: Ça y est is taught as reaching completion, readiness or understanding, not literal physical location; tasks restore y and choose it for a completed task.

entries.source_title: Ça ne fait rien = It doesn't matter (French Idiomatic Expressions)
entries.evidence: Ça ne fait rien is taught as context-sensitive reassurance with ne…rien and no added pas, distinct from no preference or completion; exercises build it and select it for a minor apology.
